/solutions/booking-systems.title: Custom Booking Systems | Orange Jelly
/solutions/booking-systems.description: Custom booking workflows that connect enquiries, confirmations and guest communication. Improve existing software or build the missing connection.
/solutions/booking-systems.h1: Booking systems that connect the guest and the team.
visible_lines: Home  →    What we build  →    Booking systems     Booking systems  Booking systems that connect the guest and the team.  We build and connect booking workflows, from the first enquiry to confirmation, changes and follow-up, so guests and staff know what happens next.  For businesses with a booking journey that depends on manual handovers or disconnected tools.   Discuss your project →        A booking journey tested in our own venue    At The Anchor, our own venue, we worked on the reason to book, the route to a confirmed table, and confirmations and reminders. The published case study explains those changes together.  The reported results belong to that wider programme. They are not a claim that a booking tool alone caused the improvement, or a promise of the same result elsewhere.  Read The Anchor booking and reminder case study        What we can build for you  We agree the scope around your customers, your team and the systems you already use.     Connect the journey you already have  Link the website, booking provider and team workflow where supported. Establish which system holds the confirmed booking and how changes reach the people who need them.    Build the missing workflow  A custom enquiry stage, private hire handover or guest information step can fill a specific gap. Agree the rules for availability, confirmation and changes before building.    Make communication clearer  Plan confirmations, reminders and follow-up around the guest journey. Agree message content, consent requirements and what staff should do when a message or connection fails.         Connect first. Replace only for a clear reason.  A new booking engine brings responsibilities for availability, changes and reliability. We first check whether your existing provider can handle the core booking while a website connection or focused application fills the gap. A replacement needs a distinct business case and agreed scope.      From the first conversation to a working build     Trace a booking from start to finish  Review enquiries, confirmations, changes, cancellations and the information your team needs. Identify the current booking record and the gaps between systems.    Agree the rules and test them  Define the supported connections and the handling of failures before launch. Test the guest route and staff handover with test bookings.    Measure the booking journey  Agree how to review completed bookings, abandoned enquiries and no-shows where data is available. Confirm who manages each connected service and future changes.         Questions before you start     Do we need to replace our booking software? +  ×   Often the useful change is around the existing provider: a better website route, information capture or staff handover. Replacement is considered only when the provider cannot meet the agreed requirements.    How will booking changes reach the team? +  ×   We agree which system is authoritative and how amendments and cancellations move through the workflow. The available connection depends on your provider, and failure handling needs to be tested.    Can the system send guest confirmations and reminders? +  ×   These can form part of the agreed scope. We check what your provider already sends, the permissions and message rules, and how staff will see failures before introducing another messaging route.    Who is responsible for third-party booking services? +  ×   We set out the responsibilities for provider accounts, subscriptions, access and ongoing maintenance in the scope. A connected service remains subject to its own terms and availability.    Does booking automation need AI? +  ×   Many booking tasks need clear rules rather than AI. We would consider AI for a suitable supporting task, such as preparing an enquiry summary, with checks appropriate to its use. Bring an idea, an existing system or a problem you want to solve.   Discuss your project →

/fractional-cmo.title: Do you need a fractional CMO? | Orange Jelly
/fractional-cmo.description: When a fractional CMO is the right hire, when it's the wrong answer, and five questions to ask first. Including when we would say hire one instead of us.
/fractional-cmo.h1: do you really need a fractional CMO?
visible_lines: Home  →    Fractional CMO     fractional leadership  do you really need a fractional  CMO ?  People search for one when growth has stalled and the in-house team is stretched. It's a sensible instinct and often the wrong kind of answer. Here's when it works, when it does not, and what to ask before you hire either of us.   Let's talk →   See the eight growth problems       what a fractional cmo actually is.    A senior marketer, part time, on your leadership team. Usually one to three days a week, usually on a rolling contract, usually somebody who has done the job full time somewhere larger.  It's a good model. It exists because a business can need senior marketing judgement long before it can justify a full-time salary for it, and the market has correctly worked out that the gap is real.        when it's the right answer.  Three cases, and they are common.     You know the problem is marketing.  Not enough demand is genuinely the thing holding you back, the rest of the business works, and what is missing is somebody senior to own it.    You have a team to lead.  There are people doing marketing already and the gap is direction, standards and someone accountable for the number.    The work is continuous.  Marketing is not a project for you, it is an operating function that needs running week after week.    If all three are true, hire one. We will say so on the call, and we can usually suggest where to look.       when it's the wrong kind of answer.     The problem crosses functions and only one of them gets a seat.  This is the common case and it is the reason this page exists. A business decides it needs marketing leadership because not enough demand is the symptom it can see. Underneath, enquiries are not turning into customers because nobody follows them up properly, margin is thin because pricing was never revisited, and the team is doing by hand what a system should do. A fractional CMO will spot that correctly and then be able to act on roughly a third of it. The other two thirds are somebody else's job, and the honest ones will tell you so. Now you are hiring a fractional COO as well, and the two of them are working out the boundary between them at your expense.    Nobody is accountable for the whole number.  Split the problem across two part-time department heads and you have split the accountability with it. Each can succeed at their own job while the thing you actually wanted does not move.    A seat is not a diagnosis.  Deciding you need a CMO is deciding what the answer is before anybody has established what the question was. That is the same mistake as buying software before defining the problem, and it is more expensive.         what we do instead.    We are not a fractional anything and we do not want a seat on your leadership team.  We take the problem, work out what is actually causing it across every part of the business it touches, and build the fix. Sometimes that's marketing. Often it's a pricing change, a process, a system, or three small things in three different places that only make sense together.  Then we leave. A piece of work that has done its job should end, which is not what a monthly retainer for a seat is designed to do.        the questions to ask either of us.  Ask these of a fractional CMO and of us. The answers will tell you which kind of help you need.     01  What would you look at first, and why that?    02  What would make you say this is not a marketing problem?    03  What does success look like, as a number, and when would we know?    04  What happens to this when you are not here any more?    05  What would make you tell me to stop paying you?    If the answers to the second and the fifth are vague, that's your answer, whoever you are talking to.        describe the problem, not the role.  Tell us what is actually happening and we'll tell you what kind of help it needs, even when that is not us. The first conversation is an hour and it's free.   Let's talk →
